column3: A formal parallel for the conditional verdict, but its subject is unrelated.
Supplies the immediately preceding covenant, its affirmation, and its obligations.
A contrary lens on choosing protective allegiance; it does not define this covenantal turning.
Repeats the conditional verdict form in a different moral domain.
Extends the aftermath into the question of seeking a religion other than God's.
Contrasts turning away with God as the believers' protecting patron.
Parallels the post-event formula and a condemnatory collective label.
States the undivided affirmation of God, revelation, and the prophets that follows the covenant.
Within the same passage, characterizes turning away as corruption rather than mere disagreement.
Shares only the collective verdict construction; its criterion is different.
Makes the passage's exclusive religious orientation explicit after the covenant sequence.
A rejected parallel from a conflict setting; it adds no clear covenantal sense.
Offers a distinct portrayal of fisq through forgetting God and self-loss.
Continues the sequence with disbelief after belief and witnessed proof.
Provides a secondary belonging criterion: following Abraham rather than claiming descent.
Pairs turning away with disbelief, sharpening one possible development of the act.
Gives the next stated consequence for the people identified in 3:82.
Names turning away but gives no covenantal object or verdict.
Applies the label fasiqun to refusing judgment by what God revealed.
Offers a contrary protection lens: God is patron of believers, unlike disbelievers.
Uses the same post-event fisq judgment after disbelief, in a different promise context.
Contrasts turning with allegiance to God, the messenger, and believers.
Shows fisq as a legal judgment, not the post-covenant condition at issue.
A contrary boundary-and-allegiance reading; it does not establish the covenant verdict.
Shares the post-event formula but concerns a distinct prohibition and penalty.
Offers a contrary picture of a harmful chosen patron, not covenantal turning itself.
Connects fisq after faith with communal wrongdoing and leaves repentance open.
Its physical turning aside is not the relevant religious turning.
Links turning away to refusal of obedience to the messenger.
Contrasts mutual patronage among wrongdoers with God's patronage of the mindful.
Specifies turning away from remembrance and preferring worldly life.
Sets human turning against God's continuing patronage and help.
Parallels departure after guidance through opposition to the messenger and another path.
Provides the positive counterpart of God's protected allies.
Characterizes hypocrites as fasiqun through persistent communal conduct.
Pairs denial with turning away in a compressed warning sequence.
Concerns redress after wrongdoing, not turning from a covenant.
Its repeated warning of nearness is only a remote secondary echo.
Frames the opposed outcomes as guidance versus loss.
Turns voluntary retreat into an eschatological summons and consequence.
Adds an emphatic warning but no covenantal object.
Denies that possessions or false patrons can shield from the final consequence.
Directly parallels turning away after a received covenantal favor and its grave loss.
Pairs denial with turning away as the orientation leading to punishment.
The positive disposition of giving and guarding adds no specific link.
Offers a contrary allegiance model: accepting a false patron opens its authority.
The temporal phrase alone has no bearing on the post-covenant turn.
Presents God's patronage as the outcome of a practiced upright path.
Directly depicts people turning away after God's judgment already stands in their scripture.
Frames the choice of a protector alongside commanded submission to God.
Shows diversion from God's remembrance and resultant loss, without covenantal specificity.
Depicts wrongdoers becoming one another's patrons through what they earned.
Contrasts faithful reception of scripture with disbelief and loss.
Defines legitimate guardianship by mindfulness rather than inherited control.
Parallels professed belief followed by turning away and a denial of true belief.
Removes every protector and intercessor before return to God.
Associates rejection of clear signs with the label fasiqun.
God's patronage appears in a separate oath matter, with little bearing on the turn.
The successful weighing formula is structurally parallel but semantically separate.
Denies any protector or intercessor apart from God, a contrary support frame.
Shares only the post-event transgression pattern in a legal rule.
Links obedience to an alternative authority with fisq and association.
Extends refusal of God's revealed judgment to the label wrongdoers.
Tests a claimed special nearness to God but does not address this covenant.
The departure is physical and narrative, not religious turning.
Denies that a close patron can benefit another on the decisive day.
Provides a general contrast between submission and deviance.
Shows allegiance to a condemned group producing an unstable identity.
Its membership and kinship ordering does not clarify post-covenant turning.
God's patronage in a household dispute is only a distant contrast.
Gives a general sin-and-Fire consequence without covenantal turning.
The gathering by leaders and records has no material connection here.
Combines judgment by revelation, turning away, sins, and the label fasiqun.
Uses fasiqun in testimony procedure, not the covenantal setting.
A return after admonition concerns a different prohibition and outcome.
Depicts misguidance as leaving no protector and no route of return.
A close covenant parallel: stipulated obligations followed by disbelief and departure from the straight way.
Records the messenger's response to turning away without explaining its status.
Contrasts genuine belief with taking other patrons and calls the latter fasiqun.
Treats turning back from religion into disbelief as ruinous in both worlds.
Pairs turning away after Islam with punishment and absence of protector or helper.
God as the praised patron is a general positive contrast only.
Names fasiqun as those who reject or are led astray by a divine sign.
Warns against following desires after knowledge and losing God's protection.
Shows disobedience through replacing what was commanded, with fisq as the outcome.
Its judgment of temporal distance adds no relevant relation.
Warns that following other communal desires after knowledge loses divine patronage.
Provides a historical pattern of retreating when a pledged duty became binding.
Depicts departure from the Lord's command and choosing hostile patrons instead.
Calls misconduct in a transaction procedure fisq, a distinct legal use.
The generic denial of wrongdoing adds no specific covenantal insight.
The temporal sequence is unrelated to turning away or fisq.
The repentance practice does not clarify the covenantal verdict.
Its conflict commands and works concern a different subject.
Within the surah, links rejection of God's signs and disobedience to lasting abasement.
A reminder of divine favor and succession, without the relevant turn or verdict.
Shows disbelief after mercy, a remote response-to-favor parallel.
The resurrection sign narrative adds no material connection.
The description of a high garden is unrelated.
The later year in the dream sequence is unrelated.
Directly defines fisq through breaking God's covenant after it has been bound.
Sets fulfillment of God's covenant as the positive counterpart to 3:82.
Shows a covenant received with a charged command to hold firmly to what was given.
Provides a close historical parallel: a received covenant followed by collective turning away.
Combines a covenantal charge with the report of hearing yet disobeying.
Shows a recurring pattern of making a covenant and then casting it aside.
Supplies an earlier formulation of undivided affirmation of the prophets.
Contrasts shared faith with turning away into division.
Restates comprehensive belief in God, messengers, and revelation as the positive stance.
Establishes the religious orientation that the surrounding passage treats as binding.
Records the messenger's response when people turn away from the call.
Directly joins turning away from obedience to God and the messenger with disbelief.
Within the same passage, frames a common commitment and marks refusal by turning away.
Affirms fulfillment of covenant and mindfulness as the opposed faithful disposition.
Warns against exchanging God's covenant and oaths for a worldly gain.
Addresses turning others from God's path while knowing its truth.
Warns believers that following hostile influence can turn them back after faith.
Challenges disbelief while God's signs and messenger are present among the audience.
Provides the communal opposite of departure: holding together to God's binding means.
Warns against division after clear proofs have arrived.
Distinguishes a believing group from the many characterized as fasiqun.
Provides a scripture covenant that was later cast behind backs for worldly exchange.
Supplies the direct counter-position to 3:84: separating among God's messengers.
Names the consequence of the messenger-separating stance.
Provides the positive counterpart: belief in God and all messengers without distinction.
Links covenant-breaking, disbelief in signs, and rejection of messengers in one sequence.
Warns against excess concerning religion and commands belief in God and His messengers.
Describes divine mercy and guidance for those who hold fast to God.
Establishes fulfillment of binding commitments as a general commanded norm.
Recalls God's covenant and the audience's pledged hearing and obedience.
Explains the aftermath of breaking a covenant: hardened hearts and distortion.
Adds a second communal covenant whose neglect produces enduring enmity.
Uses fasiqun for refusing to rule by what God revealed.
Places fisq alongside disbelief and prior revelation in a polemical setting.
Shows an Israelite covenant followed by recurrent rejection and killing of messengers.
Joins obedience to God and the messenger with the consequence of turning away.
Warns of people who take religion as diversion and abandon it.
Depicts reversal after divine guidance as being turned back on one's heels.
Shows that association nullifies the deeds even of prophetic recipients of guidance.
Contrasts God's straight path with other paths that divide from it.
Condemns splitting religion into factions, a contrary reading to the passage's unified affirmation.
Finds most prior peoples faithless to covenant and identifies them as fasiqun.
Recalls a covenantal duty attached to scripture and a repeated worldly exchange.
Shows the mountain covenant charge to hold firmly to what was given.
Supplies the primordial testimony covenant as a broad covenantal background.
Presents departure from a received sign, but without the covenantal verdict of 3:82.
Commands believers not to turn away while hearing the address.
Frames responding to God and the messenger as the life-giving opposite of refusal.
Makes turning away after proclamation a subject of warning and divine inescapability.
Contrasts competing loves with striving in God's path, only indirectly related.
Presents God's binding promise to believers as a covenantal counterpoint.
Connects trust in God with being submitted to Him.
Records a messenger's warning that turning away cannot harm God or evade succession.
Identifies fulfillment of God's covenant as a mark of the discerning.
Directly pairs breaking God's covenant after binding with curse and an evil abode.
Denies that an alternative caller had coercive authority, locating responsibility in response.
Commands fulfillment of God's covenant once it has been made binding.
Forbids breaking sworn commitments after confirmation.
Warns that using oaths deceptively can make a foot slip after it was firm.
Treats disbelief after faith as a grave reversal, while distinguishing coercion.
Makes the covenant an accountable obligation.
Warns against transgression after provision, with divine wrath as the consequence.
Recalls Adam's covenant and his failure to keep it.
Sets following God's guidance against going astray and suffering.
Depicts unstable worship that turns on its face at trial and loses both worlds.
Presents faithful keeping of trusts and covenants as a positive counterpart.
Shows people turning away when summoned to God and the messenger for judgment.
Questions whether turning from that summons arises from disease, doubt, or fear of injustice.
States the responsive alternative when believers are summoned to divine and messenger judgment.
Links obedience and mindfulness with success after the judgment summons.
Recalls a covenant with God not to turn backs, treating it as accountable.
Contrasts covenant fulfillment by believers with those still awaiting its completion.
Recalls a covenant not to serve Satan and identifies him as a manifest enemy.
Commands holding to the ordained religion and not dividing within it.
Keeps the messenger's call fixed despite others turning away from it.
Calls for response to God before the day when no turning back remains.
Shows following desire despite knowledge as an alternative to guided commitment.
Links turning away with corruption in the land and severing kinship bonds.
Depicts turning back after guidance has become clear as a satanically facilitated reversal.
Recalls a covenant already taken from believers while calling them to faith.
Warns believers against hearts hardening like earlier scripture communities over time.
Commands obedience and defines the messenger's role if people turn away.
Sets disobedience to God and His messenger under an enduring consequence.
